clients.description: Portfolio manager at a boutique investment house in Mayfair. Married with two teenage children; wants to use carry-forward to maximise pension contributions and is interested in EIS and VCT reliefs.
GP partner at a surgery in Clifton, Bristol. Grew up in Cork and moved to England in 2009. Wants to understand the tapered annual allowance and her NHS pension options.
Long-haul airline captain based at Heathrow who lives near Windsor. Divorced; pays school fees for two children and hopes to retire at 58.
French-born interior designer who runs her own studio in Edinburgh's New Town. Holds a French assurance-vie policy and needs advice on its UK tax treatment.
Daughter of Giles Pemberton, who is also a client. Organises equestrian events in the Cotswolds and is a trustee of the Pemberton family trust.
Retired arable farmer near Hereford. Plans to pass the farm to the next generation using agricultural property relief; enjoys horse racing.
Retired primary school headteacher living in Harrogate. Holds joint accounts with her husband and wants to start regular gifts to her grandchildren.
Retired consultant anaesthetist. Married to Margaret; the couple live in Harrogate. Has an NHS pension and a SIPP, and plays golf twice a week.
Employment barrister practising from chambers in Leeds. Self-employed, so wants to make larger pension contributions in good years.
Runs a plant nursery and garden shop, and recently bought the freehold of the premises. Prefers to be contacted by phone rather than email.
Dentist who owns a two-surgery practice in Leicester. Considering incorporating the practice; her brother Rohan is also a client.
Software engineer at a fintech start-up in Shoreditch, holding EMI share options. Brother of Priya Shah.
Headteacher of a secondary school in Birmingham and a member of the Teachers' Pension Scheme. Saving for her two daughters' university costs.
Solicitor and partner in the private client team at Halden & Pryce LLP in Manchester. Her partnership drawings vary from year to year.
Associate solicitor in a commercial property team. First-time buyer saving into a Lifetime ISA.
Introduced by her solicitor at Halden & Pryce after her divorce settlement. Lives in Glasgow and works part-time as a speech and language therapist.
Ukrainian-born architect at a practice in Bristol. Moved to the UK in 2016 and became a British citizen in 2022. Building up a stocks and shares ISA.
Head of data science at Corvid Analytics in Cambridge. Received a large RSU vest when the company was acquired.
Retired fire officer from Fort William who has climbed Ben Nevis more than forty times and does sponsored hill walks for charity. Wants a sustainable income from his drawdown pot.
Transferred her ISA and SIPP to us from Kestrel Wealth in 2024 after a dispute over fees. Works as a community pharmacist in Chesterfield.
Referred by John Doe; the two were at university together. Owns a small chain of independent coffee shops in Brighton.
Consultant orthopaedic surgeon. Lives in Chester with his wife and three children and does private work at weekends.
Head of operations at a logistics firm in Manchester. Enjoys classical music and long-distance running.
Freelance translator who grew up in Halesowen and now lives in York. A keen opera lover who travels to Verona every summer.
Master baker who owns three artisan bakeries in Cardiff. The business recovered strongly after COVID and he now wants to extract profits tax-efficiently.
Property developer in Surrey who collects classic cars and restores them in his own workshop. Got in touch after one of our advisers posted on LinkedIn about business relief.
Marketing director for a cosmetics brand in Guildford who studied at Goldsmiths. Inherited her late father's house; the grant of probate was issued in March.

queries.why: Assignment example: the term is John Doe's e-mail domain; c19 (climbed Ben Nevis) and c20 (came from Kestrel Wealth) each share only half of the compound and are not what the adviser wants.
The domain without '.com' in lower case; the assignment example already implies case-insensitive matching inside the e-mail.
Upper-case variant of the assignment example; letter case must not matter.
A full e-mail address identifies exactly one client; c21 only mentions the name John Doe in a referral note, so returning him for the address is wrong.
The e-mail local part identifies John Doe; c21's description says he was referred by John Doe, a reasonable but not required extra that must not outrank c01.
The full domain including '.com' is a literal part of c01's e-mail and of no other field in the corpus.
'wealth' is the second word of the compound domain neviswealth.com (c01) and a whole word in c20's description (Kestrel Wealth); both are genuine matches.
The firm name typed as two words should match the domain neviswealth.com; c19 (Ben Nevis) and c20 (Kestrel Wealth) each match one word only and are traps.
'Nevis' is the first word of c01's e-mail domain and a whole word in c19's description (climbed Ben Nevis); the single word is ambiguous, so both are legitimate.
Both clients whose first name is John are required; Sarah Johnson (prefix of a surname) and c21 (description mentions John Doe) are tolerable extras, not targets.
Surname search; c21's note mentions John Doe so he may appear below c01, but c19 and c22 only contain the word 'does' and must not be returned.
Full name of the example client; c21's description literally contains 'John Doe' so he is tolerable below c01, while c22 (a John who 'does' private work) only matches by accident and is wrong.
Same person typed surname first; word order must not change the answer given for 'John Doe'.
Leading, trailing and repeated spaces must be normalised; the answer equals that for 'John Doe'.
Robert Ashworth is known as Bob, which appears only in his e-mail local part (bob.ashworth); together with the surname it identifies him.
Three clients share the surname (a married couple and an unrelated barrister) and all must be returned; Hattie Greaves (c10) has a different surname that is merely contained in it.

The named client must come first; her husband c08 matches both words (surname plus 'Married to Margaret') so he is tolerable, but unrelated Lucy Hargreaves (c09) matches the surname only and is wrong.
'Surname, Forename' as copied from UK admin lists; the comma and order must be ignored, so the answer equals 'Margaret Hargreaves'.
Two unrelated clients are called Priya and both are required; c12's description mentions his sister Priya Shah, which is tolerable, but he is not a Priya.
Only Priya Shah is both a Priya and a dentist; the other Priya (c13) and her brother c12 match one word only and are not what the adviser is looking for.
Exact stored name with a fada and an apostrophe; Mark Sullivan (c03) matches only part of the surname and is wrong for a full-name query.
Typed without the accent; her e-mail (s.osullivan) does not contain the first name, so only accent-insensitive name matching finds Siobhán.
The apostrophe surname must be matched safely and exactly; Mark Sullivan carries the anglicised form of the same name, so he is tolerable but must rank below Siobhán.
Both names typed without accents; her e-mail contains 'renee' but not 'lefevre', so the surname must be matched accent-insensitively against Lefèvre.
Reverse case: the adviser types the diaeresis but the client is stored as 'Zoe', so accent folding must be applied to the query as well as to the data.
Double-barrelled surname typed with a space instead of the hyphen; her father Giles Pemberton (c06) matches only the first half and is not who the adviser wants.
'Hale' is a full part of the double-barrelled surname Pemberton-Hale; c24 merely grew up in Halesowen, a different word.
Surname stored in Cyrillic must be found when typed exactly as stored.
Lower-case Cyrillic: case-insensitive matching has to work beyond ASCII (an ASCII-only LIKE/lower() fails here).
The Latin spelling an English-speaking adviser would type appears in her e-mail (oksana.melnyk), so this is a direct e-mail match.
Employer named in c18's description and e-mail domain; c25's 'COVID' is a different word one letter away and must not be returned.
c14 and c15 are solicitors; c16's description mentions 'her solicitor', so the word matches but she is not a solicitor and is only tolerable.

No description contains 'doctor', but the GP, the retired anaesthetist and the orthopaedic surgeon are doctors and the dentist (courtesy title Dr) is tolerable; only semantic matching finds them, hence nice.
Only c22 lives in Chester; Manchester (c14, c23) and Chesterfield (c20) merely contain the letters and are different places.
c02 and c17 mention Bristol in their descriptions; c10's handle 'thepottingshedbristol' is only in a social link, a field the assignment does not list, so she is tolerable but not required.
c08's description says he plays golf; c03's Instagram handle 'markplaysgolf' hints at golf too, but social links are outside the listed fields, so he is tolerable only.
c24 is an opera lover; c23's 'operations' only starts with the same letters and is unrelated.
c26 collects classic cars; c23 'enjoys classical music', which shares a prefix but is not what the adviser wants.
Only c19's description mentions the mountain; John Doe's domain contains 'nevis' but has nothing to do with Ben Nevis, so c01 is wrong here.
Margaret Hargreaves lives in Harrogate; her husband c08 also matches both words ('Married to Margaret', Harrogate) and is tolerable, but the client actually called Margaret must be first.

Clients tied to this law firm: c14 works there (description and e-mail), c15 works there (only his haldenpryce e-mail domain shows it) and c16 was introduced by its solicitor; the '&' must also survive URL encoding.
Two colleagues share this e-mail domain and both are required; c16 only mentions the firm in her description and has no address there, so she is not what a domain search asks for.
The married couple share a family e-mail domain; Lucy Hargreaves (c09) has the surname but a different domain and is wrong.
A full address identifies one client even though his colleague c14 shares the domain; c14 (and c27, whose description mentions a 'grant') must not be returned.
The named client must be first; his daughter c05 mentions 'Giles Pemberton' in her description and has Pemberton in her surname, so she is tolerable below him.
Giles has the surname and Arabella has it as one half of her double-barrelled surname Pemberton-Hale; neither clearly outranks the other.
Mark Sullivan has exactly this surname and must be first; Siobhán O'Sullivan has the same name after the O' prefix, so she is tolerable but not required.
Same word in different fields: Ruth Baker's surname is the strongest match and must come first, while c25 is a master baker by profession, which is also a plausible intent.
Oliver Grant must come first; c27's description mentions a 'grant of probate', a literal match in an unrelated sense, so she is tolerable only.
Swapped letters in the first name; fuzzy matching should still put John Doe first, with c21 (whose note mentions John Doe) tolerable and the other John (c22) wrong.
Misspelt surname (ee for ea); all three Hargreaves are intended, while Hattie Greaves (c10) is a different, shorter surname.
Missing letter in the assignment's example domain; a fuzzy match should still find John Doe.
The classic ie/ei swap of Whitfield; no other client has a similar name.
The handle appears only in c03's Instagram link; the assignment lists e-mail, name and description, so not searching links is no defect, but an adviser typing the handle clearly means him.

An adviser pasting a profile URL wants to know whether that person is a client; the URL is stored only in c10's social links (links are not a listed field, hence nice), and the Hargreaves clients merely contain 'greaves'.
Only c26's description mentions LinkedIn (how he found the firm); the linkedin.com host in a dozen clients' profile URLs is boilerplate, so returning those clients is noise.
No client is called John Smith; the two Johns match one word only and c27's 'Goldsmiths' merely contains 'smith', so the correct answer is an empty list.
No client has the surname Smith; 'Goldsmiths' in c27's description contains the letters but names a college, not the person sought.
No client is an actuary or mentions actuarial work; a search that always returns its nearest neighbours (e.g. pure vector similarity) would wrongly show unrelated professionals.
A two-letter query that is a complete surname: Daniel Ng must be found, but the many words that merely contain 'ng' (living, running, Long-haul) must not be returned.
A two-letter professional abbreviation that appears as a word only in c02's description ('GP partner'); a minimum-length rule must not drop it.
A single letter means nothing to the adviser and substring matching would return nearly every client, so an empty list is the correct result.
A whitespace-only query has no search terms; after trimming, a naive LIKE '%%' would return every client, so the result must be empty.
Every e-mail contains '@', but no adviser wants the whole client list for it; punctuation alone must give an empty result.
'%' is the SQL LIKE wildcard: unescaped it matches every client, while the literal character appears in no client field.
Classic SQL-injection tautology; with parameterised queries it is plain text that matches no client, so the result must be empty, never the full table or a 500.
Injection attempt that must be treated as literal text; it matches no client (the word 'client' in two descriptions is not what was typed) and the table must survive.
Script markup matches no client and must neither error nor be reflected unescaped; the correct result is an empty list.
A lone backslash is PostgreSQL's default LIKE escape character and makes an unescaped pattern invalid (a common 500); no client field contains one.
A NUL byte (sent as %00) cannot be stored in PostgreSQL text and often triggers a 500; it must be handled gracefully and match nothing.
